title: How to Use a Teleprompter on Snapchat Without It Ending Up in the Snap
seoTitle: Teleprompter for Snapchat: Read Your Script on Camera
author: Nishant Hada
content:
Snapchat is a camera before it is anything else, and that is exactly what makes a scripted Snap hard. There is no notes pane, no prompter in the record screen, and nowhere to look but the lens. So you either memorise the whole thing or you shoot it eleven times.

A floating teleprompter fixes it from the outside. **[CueCard Teleprompter](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/snapchat/)** puts your script in a small window that sits on top of Snapchat while Snapchat records normally underneath it. You read; the Snap comes out of the app it always came out of.

### What actually goes wrong when you script a Snap

* **You lose the thread after the hook.** The first line is the one you rehearsed. Line four is the one you invent, badly, and then restart from the top.
* **Your eyes give it away.** Reading off a sticky note beside the phone drags your eye-line off the lens by a visible margin. Viewers cannot name what is wrong, but they can feel it.
* **Camera roll is not the same shot.** Filming elsewhere and uploading means losing the in-app feel that Spotlight and Stories are built around, and adds an export step you did not want.
* **Takes drift long.** Without a clock running, a “quick” Snap turns into forty seconds of throat-clearing before the point.

### Put the script on the glass instead

1. **Write it in CueCard and save it.** One hook line, one idea, one ask. Named scripts stay in your library, so a series can be shot back to back.
2. **Set the pace in lines per minute.** Most people speak between 120 and 160 words a minute. Nudge the speed between takes until the script moves at the rate you actually talk, rather than making you chase it.
3. **Shape the window for the shot.** Pick 16:9, 4:3 or 1:1, set its text size, and park it as high on the screen as it will go — as close to the front camera as you can get it, and no bigger than it needs to be.
4. **Use a start delay.** The countdown counts you in, so the first line is not the one you fumble while reaching for the record button.
5. **Open Snapchat and film.** The prompter stays on top. It is a window on your screen, not something in front of the lens, so it is not in the footage.

### Cues, so you read direction instead of speaking it

Write `[cue smile]`, `[cue hold for two]` or `[cue look up]` in the middle of a line and CueCard draws it in its own colour. Your eye takes it in as a stage direction rather than a word to say. For Snapchat, where the whole clip lives or dies on the first second, `[cue slower]` right after the hook is worth more than another rewrite.

The word you are meant to be on is lit as the script scrolls, which is the part that matters for a talking-to-camera Snap: you can glance at the lens for a full beat, come back, and your eye lands in the right place instead of hunting through the paragraph.

### Keep the glance short

The distance between your eye-line and the lens is the entire trick. Small window, parked directly under the front camera, text just big enough to read at arm’s length. On camera it reads as someone thinking, not someone reading. That is as close to a beam-splitter rig as you get without buying one.

CueCard Teleprompter is free on **[iPhone and iPad](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/ios/)** — iOS 17 or later, no subscription, open source — with **[Android](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/android/)** coming soon. The same window floats over **[Instagram](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/instagram/)**, **[TikTok](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/tiktok/)** and everything else you post to, so one script covers the whole day’s filming. **[Get it here](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/)**.

title: Why Your Reels Look Like You’re Reading — and How to Fix the Eye-Line
seoTitle: Instagram Reels Teleprompter: Stop Looking Like You’re Reading
author: Nishant Hada
content:
Nobody watching a Reel thinks “that person is reading a script.” They think “something is off” and swipe. The tell is almost always the same: your eyes are travelling somewhere the camera is not, and the audience clocks it in under a second without ever knowing why.

The fix is not memorising harder. It is moving the words closer to the lens and slowing the take down enough that reading and talking stop competing. Here is how to set that up on a phone, with **[CueCard Teleprompter](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/instagram/)** or with anything else that floats a script over Instagram.

### The three tells, in order of how badly they hurt

* **The sweep.** Your eyes track left to right across a wide line of text. A phone-width paragraph is the worst possible shape to read on camera. Narrow the window; short lines mean a shorter sweep.
* **The drop.** You look down at a page, a second phone or a laptop below the frame. Anything under the lens turns your face into a shot of your eyelids. Park the script high, right under the front camera.
* **The catch-up.** The script is moving faster than you talk, so you speed up, run out of breath, and the last third of the Reel sounds rushed. Set the pace to your voice, not the other way round.

### Set the pace to your actual speaking speed

CueCard scrolls in lines per minute rather than a vague slider, so you can dial it in and keep it. Start slower than feels right — most people read comfortably a little under the 120–160 words a minute they speak at — record thirty seconds, and adjust once. Two takes to find your number, and every Reel after that starts correct.

The current word is highlighted as the script moves. That is what buys you the lens: you can hold eye contact through a whole sentence, come back, and land exactly where you left off instead of scanning for your place.

### Write for the mouth, not the page

Long sentences read fine and speak badly. Break the script into lines you can say in one breath, and put the direction in the script itself:

* `[cue pause]` after the hook, so the first idea has room to land.
* `[cue smile]` before the ask, because you will forget.
* `[cue slower]` anywhere you know you rush — the price, the name, the URL.

Cues are drawn in their own colour and are never part of the words you say. They are notes from you to you, in the middle of the line where you need them.

### The physical setup, in one minute

1. Phone at eye height, not on a desk pointing up at you.
2. Floating window set to 16:9, 4:3 or 1:1 — whichever keeps it out of the part of the frame you care about — and pushed to the top of the screen.
3. Text size up until you can read it at arm’s length without leaning in. Leaning in is a tell too.
4. Start delay on, so the countdown counts you in and take one starts on your hook rather than on you reaching for the button.
5. Timer set to the length you are cutting to. Knowing at record time that you ran nineteen seconds long saves the discovery in the edit.

### Then film in Instagram, like always

The prompter floats above Instagram, so the Reel is still captured, cropped and posted by Instagram. Nothing exports, nothing round-trips, and the prompter is a window on your screen rather than an object in front of the lens — it is not in the footage.

CueCard Teleprompter is free on **[iPhone and iPad](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/ios/)**, running on iOS 17 or later, with **[Android](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/android/)** on the way. It works the same over **[TikTok](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/tiktok/)**, **[YouTube](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/youtube/)** and **[Snapchat](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/snapchat/)**, so a script you fix once is fixed everywhere. **[See it on your phone](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/)**, or read how **[content creators](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/content-creators/)** set it up.

title: A TikTok Teleprompter That Isn’t Trapped Inside TikTok
seoTitle: TikTok Teleprompter: One Script, Every App You Film In
author: Nishant Hada
content:
A prompter built into one app’s record screen works right up until you film somewhere else — and creators film somewhere else constantly. The native camera for a better-looking take, an editor for the version with b-roll, a live stream, a second platform that gets the same script tomorrow. The words should follow you across all of it.

That is the whole argument for a floating teleprompter. **[CueCard Teleprompter](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/tiktok/)** is a window that sits on top of whatever app is in front of it, so the same script reads over TikTok, over your camera, over a stream, without being rewritten or pasted anywhere new.

### Where an in-app prompter runs out

* **You are filming in the camera app.** Shooting outside TikTok for the footage you want, then uploading, means the in-app prompter is not there at all.
* **You are going live.** A live stream is not the record screen, and lives are precisely where forgetting your third point costs the most.
* **You are posting the same script twice.** A cut for TikTok and a version for Reels means retyping the script into a second app’s prompter, and the two drift apart on the first edit.
* **You need direction, not just words.** “Say this” is half the job. “Smile here, pause here, slow down for the price” is the half that makes it watchable.

### One script, saved once

Write the script in CueCard, name it, and it stays in your library. Open it tomorrow for the second cut, next week for the follow-up, or right now for the take you are about to reshoot for the fourth time. Nothing is retyped, and there is only ever one copy to edit.

Inside the script, cues carry the delivery. `[cue hook]`, `[cue pause]`, `[cue point at the product]` — each drawn in its own colour, each unmistakably a direction rather than a line. Type `[` and the tag writes itself. You choose the colour, so cues stand as far from the script as you want.

### Making 30 seconds actually fit into 30 seconds

Short-form runs on length discipline, and the two settings that enforce it are both in the app:

* **A start delay** counts you in, so the recording does not open on you reaching for the button.
* **A timer** counts down while you talk. You find out you ran eleven seconds long while you are still standing there, not in the edit.

Set the scroll speed in lines per minute and match it to how you actually talk. The word you are on is highlighted as it moves, so the gaps where you look straight down the lens do not cost you your place.

### The setup that keeps it off camera

The floating window can be 16:9, 4:3 or 1:1, with its own text size, and you park it where it does not cover the part of the frame you are composing. It is a window on your screen, not something in front of the lens, so it is not in the footage. If you are screen recording rather than filming, hide it first.

Push it as close to the front camera as it will go and keep it small. Short glance, short tell.

### Get it

CueCard Teleprompter is free on **[iPhone and iPad](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/ios/)** — iOS 17 or later, no subscription, MIT licensed and open source on GitHub — with **[Android](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/android/)** coming soon. The same window floats over **[Instagram](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/instagram/)**, **[YouTube](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/youtube/)**, **[Twitch](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/twitch/)** and everything else.

title: One Screen, No Second Monitor: Reading Notes on Zoom and Google Meet
seoTitle: Speaker Notes on Zoom and Google Meet With One Screen
author: Nishant Hada
content:
Presenter view solves the notes problem only if you have somewhere to put it. On a single laptop screen there is nowhere: share the whole screen and your notes go out with the deck, share one window and your notes end up behind the thing you are sharing. Most people end up reading off a phone propped against a mug, which is its own kind of visible.

**[CueCard for Mac and Windows](https://cuecard.dev/desktop/)** takes the other route. It is a floating notes window that is excluded from screen capture, so it can sit in the middle of the screen you are sharing and still not be in what Zoom or Google Meet sends out.

### Why the usual workarounds are worse than they look

* **Share a window, not the screen.** It works until you need to switch to a demo, a browser tab or a second app — and then you are stopping the share mid-sentence to start another one.
* **Share a tab in Google Meet.** Clean, but your notes window is now behind a full-screen slideshow on the only display you have.
* **Second monitor.** Fine when you have one. It also drags your eye-line off the webcam by a wide margin, which reads as distraction to everyone on the call.
* **Notes on your phone.** Every glance down is a glance down, and phones are unmistakable on camera.

### How the invisible window works

CueCard is hidden at the operating-system level rather than per app. Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Webex, Slack huddles, Discord, and screen recordings too — the notes are excluded from capture, so it is not a list you have to be on. There is a “Show in Screen Capture” switch in Settings; leave it off and run one practice call to confirm it behaves as you expect on your machine.

Because it is invisible rather than merely out of the way, you can put it where you actually want it: high on the screen, right under your webcam, so your eyes stay near the lens the whole call.

### Timing and cues, written into the notes

* `[time 05:00]` counts down on screen. A thirty-minute slot stays thirty minutes, and you find out you are over while you can still cut something.
* `[cue slow down]`, `[cue ask for questions]`, `[cue share the doc]` are highlighted in the cue colour and never read aloud — direction, in the middle of the line where you need it.
* Transparency fades the window back over your deck or brings it forward, and it follows your system light or dark theme.

### Setting it up before your next call

1. Download CueCard for **[macOS or Windows](https://cuecard.dev/desktop/#download)** — macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 or later, free and open source.
2. Paste your notes in. Presenting from PowerPoint, Keynote, a PDF or nothing at all is fine; if you use **[Google Slides](https://cuecard.dev/google-slides/)**, the extension syncs the notes for the slide you are on as you advance.
3. Drop `[time]` markers on the sections that always run long, and `[cue]` tags on the moments you always forget.
4. Park the window under your webcam and start the call. Share your entire screen if you want to — that is the point.

Then present on **[Zoom](https://cuecard.dev/zoom/)**, **[Google Meet](https://cuecard.dev/google-meet/)** or **[Microsoft Teams](https://cuecard.dev/microsoft-teams/)** with the deck going out and nothing else.

Filming rather than presenting? The **[phone app](https://cuecard.dev/mobile/)** is the same idea pointed at a camera: a prompter that floats over Instagram, TikTok or whatever else you record in, free on iPhone and iPad.

title: Google Slides Speaker Notes: Off the Shared Screen, Onto Yours
seoTitle: Google Slides Speaker Notes While Screen Sharing
author: Nishant Hada
content:
Google Slides puts your speaker notes in a presenter view window, and presenter view is a window like any other — which means the moment you share your entire screen, your notes are part of the presentation. Sharing only the slideshow window keeps them private, right up until you need to switch to a demo and have to stop and restart the share.

The **[CueCard browser extension](https://cuecard.dev/google-slides/)** takes the notes out of that window entirely. It reads the speaker notes for the slide you are on and hands them to the desktop app, which is excluded from screen capture. Your notes are on your screen, following your deck, and not in the share.

### What presenter view does not give you

* **Nowhere safe to put it.** Two windows, one display, and a share that has to include one of them.
* **A wall of text.** The notes pane prints your whole note for the slide at one size, with nothing marked as more important than anything else.
* **No clock per section.** There is a timer for the talk. There is nothing telling you that slide six was supposed to be ninety seconds and has been four minutes.
* **It breaks when you leave.** Alt-tab out of a full-screen slideshow to show something and the arrangement you set up falls apart.

### How the sync works

1. Install **[CueCard for macOS or Windows](https://cuecard.dev/desktop/#download)** — free, open source, macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 or later.
2. Add the browser extension for **Chrome**, **Firefox** or **Safari**. The Safari one is installed by the macOS app; the others come from their own stores, linked on the **[Google Slides page](https://cuecard.dev/google-slides/)**.
3. Open your presentation and present as you always do. The notes for the current slide appear in CueCard and change as you advance.

No copying, no second document to keep in step with the deck. Edit a note in Slides and the note you read is the note you edited.

### Then add the two things Slides has no field for

Speaker notes are just text, which means they can carry more than words:

* `[time 02:00]` on a slide counts down on screen while you talk it. Put one on every section that has ever run long and the whole talk stays inside its slot.
* `[cue take a breath]`, `[cue click the demo]`, `[cue hand over to Sam]` are drawn in the cue colour and never read out — they are directions to you, sitting in the middle of the note where you need them.

Fade the window back with the transparency control if it is sitting over your deck, or bring it forward when the room goes quiet and you need the words.

### It is invisible, not just tidy

CueCard is excluded from screen capture at the operating-system level, so it stays out of **[Zoom](https://cuecard.dev/zoom/)**, **[Google Meet](https://cuecard.dev/google-meet/)**, **[Microsoft Teams](https://cuecard.dev/microsoft-teams/)**, Webex, Slack huddles and screen recordings alike. Share your entire screen, switch to a browser, run the demo, come back to the deck — the notes never appear in any of it. Check that “Show in Screen Capture” is off in Settings and do one practice call to see it for yourself.

### And if the deck is not in Slides

The sync is a convenience, not a requirement. Paste your notes straight into CueCard and present from PowerPoint, Keynote, a PDF, a browser or nothing at all — the window behaves identically. **[Download CueCard](https://cuecard.dev/desktop/)** and get your notes off the shared screen.

### Why Choose CueCard Over Other Teleprompters?

CueCard doesn’t just mirror standard teleprompter features; it’s built specifically for modern workflows. Teachers, marketers and students can maintain eye contact and control pacing during presentations. Creators and vloggers can film hands-free videos with notes floating over the camera. Because everything runs locally and is open-source, your notes remain private.
